characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: JEOL 2010 microscope; foils prepared by twin-jet electropolishing in 25% nitric acid in methanol at about 20 V and −30 °C
characterization_methods.key_findings: Deformation substructure consists of straight, near-screw-oriented superdislocations (2 (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials) plus numerous edge dislocation dipoles and loops (Fig. 14); stepped structures and dislocation pairs from reactions (Fig. 15); reaction-produced dislocation pairs together with APBII residual-contrast fringes traversing the area (Fig. 16).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Dislocations imaged in Bright Field and Weak Beam modes; planar (shear or thermal) faults observed in various dark field modes; Burgers vectors identified using a variety of g vectors generally in Bright Field; ±g imaging pairs used to certify dipoles
characterization_methods.purpose: Examine the dislocation structures produced by room-temperature straining to 2–3% in Fe–30% Al

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Superdislocations are often rather straight in screw orientations, with reactions between dislocations leading to stepped structures; dislocation pairs observed (Figs. 15 and 16) are the result of dislocation reactions and do not correspond to the partials of the glissile superdislocations.

interfaces.interface_notes: For Fe–30% Al the APBI fault energy is sufficiently high that partials remain closely coupled; the dislocation pairs seen are reaction products (stepped structures) rather than the partials of glissile superdislocations.
interfaces.phase_evolution: Movement of the (1/2)⟨111⟩ partial pairs destroys some of the DO3 order during deformation, leaving residual APBII contrast fringes across the deformed areas.

phase_interfaces.coherence: APBI fault energy is sufficiently high at 30% Al that the separation of the (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials constituting the superdislocation is small; parallel image pairs correspond to short or long dipole dislocation pairs, not separated partials.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Deformation occurs by movement of superdislocations composed of 2 (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials that are perfect superdislocations for the B2 lattice but imperfect for the DO3 lattice (trailing APBII faults); superdislocations are often rather straight in screw orientations.

processing_steps.method: standard induction melting in an alumina crucible under inert gas followed by drop casting into a 25 mm diameter cylindrical copper mould
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Binary alloy with 30% Al (atomic percent throughout); produces samples with grain size of the order of 0.25 mm.

Cooling after solidification sufficiently slow to allow a high degree of B2 order for Al-rich alloys and a good degree of DO3 order for alloys containing 25–30% Al; confirms this state of order by strong superlattice spots and coarse DO3 domains in TEM.

Samples cut by spark machining as 3 mm diameter or 5 mm × 5 mm square cross-section, height twice the diameter/width; flat surfaces polished on 1500 grade abrasive paper; tested at room temperature to a strain of 2–3% at a nominal strain rate of 3×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; compression axis parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples; smooth onset of plasticity with no discrete yield points and slightly curved stress–strain behaviour.

processing_steps.method: thin foils cut with a diamond saw from the centre of the deformed samples perpendicular to the stress axis and prepared by twin-jet electropolishing in 25% nitric acid in methanol at about 20 V and −30 °C
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Foils examined in a JEOL 2010 microscope; dislocations imaged in Bright Field and Weak Beam modes and planar (shear or thermal) faults in various dark field modes.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Compression axis parallel to the cylinder axis of the cast samples; smooth onset of plasticity with no discrete yield points; stress–strain behaviour slightly curved.
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: 3 mm diameter or 5 mm × 5 mm square cross-section samples of height twice the diameter/width

defects.description: Invariably superdislocations produced by the same 2 (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials; often rather straight and in near-screw orientations.
defects.type: superdislocations of the B2 lattice composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials

defects.description: Many edge dislocation dipoles and loops; the paired dislocations marked d in Fig. 14 (right) are generally dipole segments and loops.
defects.type: edge dislocation dipoles and dipole loops

defects.description: Superdislocations often rather straight in screw orientations with reactions between dislocations leading to stepped structures; the dislocation pairs are the result of dislocation reactions and do not correspond to the partials of the glissile superdislocations.
defects.type: dislocation pairs / stepped structures from dislocation reactions

defects.description: A large number of fringes traverse the entire area studied; due to residual contrast of the APBII fringes produced during deformation of this weakly DO3-ordered material because the pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials destroy this order during movement.

phases_present.morphology: high degree of B2 order for Al-rich alloys
weak DO3 order for Fe–30% Al; fine DO3 domains or partial disorder

microstructure_list.region: centre of the deformed compression sample (thin foil cut perpendicular to the stress axis)

structures.overall_structure: Weakly DO3-ordered Fe–30% Al after room-temperature deformation to 2–3%; deformation occurs by movement of superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (perfect superdislocations of the B2 lattice), with many straight near-screw dislocations plus numerous edge dislocation dipoles and loops.

unmapped_findings: Fe–30% Al is described as a weakly DO3-ordered material that deforms by the movement of superdislocations composed of two (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials (perfect superdislocations of the B2 lattice).

For Fe–30% Al the APBI fault energy is sufficiently high that the separation of the partials constituting the superdislocation is small; the parallel image pairs visible in Fig. 14 (right) all correspond to short or long dipole dislocation pairs rather than separated partials.

Dislocation pairs observed in deformed Fe–30% Al (Figs. 15 and 16) are the result of dislocation reactions and do not correspond to the partials of the glissile superdislocations; reactions lead to stepped structures.

Fringes traversing the deformed Fe–30% Al areas (Fig. 16) are residual APBII contrast, produced because the pairs of (1/2)⟨111⟩ partials destroy some of the DO3 order during movement in this weakly DO3-ordered material.

In situ straining of a Fe–30% Al alloy (Ref. [32], cited in b0056) showed spontaneous formation of dipole debris behind moving screw dislocations without apparent intersection with any forest dislocation or other debris.

The work hardening rate of Fe–Al alloys shows a sharp maximum near Fe–28% Al, coinciding with an equally strong maximum in elastic anisotropy; this is attributed to strong Peierls forces for compositions close to 25–30% Al rather than to elastic anisotropy itself.
